### Observed differences

- All six qualifying evidence items concern resource assignment, and the screening comparison points squarely at resources: 6 of 6 tested resource units qualified where only about 0.003 were expected by chance (roughly 2000 times the chance expectation), while control flow produced 0 of 35 units (about 0.17 expected) and timing 0 of 32 (about 0.016 expected). [screening]
- In the earlier window, each of the six affected activities (A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A22) was handled by a broad mix of resources: the most-used resource, User_32, held only about 11–16% of assignments, and roughly 40–50% of the work was spread over a long tail of occasional resources. In the later window, this mix is replaced on every one of these activities by a largely different set of resources. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- A01 shows the sharpest shift: from a spread pattern (top share about 13%, long tail about 48%) to complete concentration, with User_47 handling all A01 assignments in the later window. [ASSIGN001]
- On A03, A13/A14, A17 and A22, the previously dominant resources drop out or shrink, and a new group of about ten resources — including User_23 — takes the largest shares, roughly 5–11% each, while the long tail stays at a similar size (about 35–52%). The redistribution is largest for A22 (dissimilarity 0.66 on a 0–1 scale) and moderate for the others (0.40–0.44). [ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- A13 and A14 have identical before and after profiles, so they most likely reflect one shared allocation pattern rather than two independent changes. [ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004]
- Every item's difference is larger than in all but about 1 in 2000 random re-splits of the pooled data, and the profiles rest on substantial support: about 200 traces per window for A01 and A03, roughly 240–260 observations for A13/A14 and A17, and about 125 and 113 for A22. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports a change in resource allocation as a possibility: in the later window, assignment work on A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 was reallocated from a former group of resources, previously led by User_32 with per-activity shares of roughly 11–16%, to a largely different group that includes User_23, and A01 moved from a spread pattern to being handled entirely by User_47. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, screening]

Supporting signs: the resource family produced six qualifying items against a chance expectation of about 0.003, control flow and timing produced none, all six items point in the same direction (former group out, new group in), and each difference exceeds about 1999 of 2000 random re-splits. [screening, ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

Limitations: the resource codes are anonymous, so the evidence shows who executed the work but not why; an important competing explanation it cannot rule out is that the case mix itself changed — different kinds of cases reaching different resources — rather than a reallocation of the same work. A13 and A14 share one profile, so the six items are not fully independent, and A22, the largest shift, has the smallest support (about 125 and 113 observations). [ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN006]
